newsitem.title: USA: Jackson keeps options open for 2000 run.
newsitem.headline: Jackson keeps options open for 2000 run.

text.p: Civil rights leader Jesse Jackson is keeping his options open for another presidential bid in 2000, the Washington Post reported in Sunday editions.

Jackson, who ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1984 and 1988, told the newspaper in an interview last week that the considerations that kept him out of the race in 1992 and 1996 would not apply next time.

"It's premature to make that decision," he said. "But I have protected my eligibility to run by continuing to work, by being a voice of conscience and hope and by registering voters and by supporting the Democratic Party."
Jackson said he did not run in 1992 because he felt then-Arkansas governor Bill Clinton had a chance to beat incumbent President George Bush and "stop the Reagan-Bush connection."
In 1996, he did not run to avoid splitting the ticket and handing votes to Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole.
"The scenario (for 2000) is very different than it was in '92 and '96 ... there will be a contest for the heart and soul of the party," he told the paper.
Another presidential bid by Jackson would be bad news for Vice President Al Gore, who is widely expected to seek his party's nomination in 2000.

"We are very close," Jackson said of Gore. "I respect him, his integrity, his ability. We are members of the same party. The issues I'm raising are not personal. This has to do with direction and priorities."
